question.problem:
A reactor initially holds $520\,\text{L}$ of a chemical solution containing $8\,\text{kg}$ of reactant.
A pure solvent is poured into the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the reactor at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ Which differential equation best describes the amount of reactant $Q,$ in kilograms, in the reactor $t$ minutes after the solvent begins to be added?
question.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which reactant enters the reactor minus the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which reactant enters the reactor.

First, note that the incoming solvent (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of reactant) enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *reactant* enters the reactor is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (16\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.

Now, to find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$

- The reactor initially contains $520\,\text{L}$ of solution.

- Solvent enters the reactor at a rate of $16\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $16t\,\text{L}$ have entered the reactor.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the reactor at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $20t\,\text{L}$ have left the reactor.

As a result, the volume of solution in the reactor after $t$ minutes is 

$$
520+16t-20t=(520-4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the mass of reactant in the reactor, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{20Q}{520-4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{130-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

Finally, the rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{130-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{5}{130-t}Q=0.\end{aligned}
$$
